profiles.hook: Anca Dragan is a computer scientist working on human-robot interaction and AI alignment. Born in Braila, Romania, she studied at Jacobs University Bremen before earning her PhD in robotics at Carnegie Mellon University. She joined the electrical engineering and computer sciences faculty at UC Berkeley, where she founded the InterACT Lab to study how autonomous systems can move and act legibly around people, and became a co-principal investigator of the Center for Human-Compatible AI. She spent six years advising Waymo on learning-based safety systems for self-driving cars. In 2017, MIT Technology Review named her to its Innovators Under 35 list for this work. She has since gone on leave from Berkeley to lead AI Safety and Alignment research at Google DeepMind.
profiles.name: Anca Dragan
profiles.moniker: Human-robot interaction and AI alignment researcher

profiles.hook: Chelsea Finn is a computer scientist working at the intersection of robotics and machine learning. She earned a BS in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT, then a PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley, where she helped develop Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), a widely used algorithm for training models that adapt quickly to new tasks. She then worked as a researcher across Google's Brain and DeepMind teams before becoming an Assistant Professor of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. There she leads the IRIS Lab, which studies how robots and other agents can develop broadly intelligent behavior through learning and interaction. More recently, she co-founded Physical Intelligence, a startup building general-purpose foundation models for robots. Her work has earned the ACM Doctoral Dissertation Award, an ONR Young Investigator Award, and a Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers.

profiles.hook: Danijar Hafner is a machine learning researcher known for developing the Dreamer family of world-model algorithms for reinforcement learning. He completed a Master of Research at University College London and the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, mentored by Timothy Lillicrap and Karl Friston, then earned his PhD at the University of Toronto advised by Jimmy Ba as a Vanier Scholar. During this time he was also a visiting student at UC Berkeley under Pieter Abbeel and completed a multi-year internship at Google Brain. He created PlaNet and the original Dreamer algorithm, which learns behaviors by imagining future outcomes inside a learned latent world model, then led development of DreamerV2 and DreamerV3. He is now a Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind, where he continues to work on world models, temporal abstraction, and scalable self-improvement for AI agents.

profiles.hook: David Silver is a computer scientist known for leading reinforcement learning research at DeepMind. He earned his PhD at the University of Alberta under reinforcement learning pioneer Richard Sutton, then became a professor at University College London while also leading DeepMind's reinforcement learning research. He led the teams behind DeepMind's Atari-playing deep Q-network, AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero, and MuZero, a series of systems that mastered Go, chess, shogi, and Atari games through self-play and learned models. He later contributed to AlphaFold's protein structure predictions and to AlphaProof, a system that reached silver-medal-level performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad. He has since stepped back from leading DeepMind's reinforcement learning team to become CEO of a new venture, Ineffable Intelligence, while remaining a professor at UCL.

profiles.hook: Gill Pratt is a roboticist known for his work directing robotics research at DARPA and for leading Toyota's artificial intelligence research effort. He earned his PhD at MIT, later teaching robotics there and at Olin College of Engineering. Before joining Toyota, he served as a program manager at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, where he oversaw robotics programs including the DARPA Robotics Challenge. In 2015, Toyota Motor Corporation created the Toyota Research Institute, based in Los Altos, California, and appointed him to lead it. Under his leadership TRI has conducted research on artificial intelligence, robotics, and automated driving, and he has continued in senior technical leadership roles at Toyota focused on human-centered mobility and automation.

profiles.hook: Julian Schrittwieser is an Austrian software engineer and AI researcher. He worked at Google DeepMind for years, where he was a key contributor to AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero and the lead author of MuZero, a reinforcement learning algorithm that mastered Go, chess, shogi, and Atari games while learning its own model of each game's rules. He went on to work on AlphaTensor, AlphaDev, and AlphaCode, and later on AlphaProof, which reached silver-medal-level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. In 2025 he moved to Anthropic to continue AI research. He also writes a technical blog, at julian.ac, about AI progress and software engineering.

profiles.hook: Marc Raibert is a roboticist known as the founder of Boston Dynamics. He held research and faculty positions at Carnegie Mellon University and MIT, where he ran the MIT Leg Lab studying dynamic, legged locomotion in robots. In 1992 he spun the lab's work out of MIT to found Boston Dynamics, joined soon after by Robert Playter. Under his leadership the company built a series of dynamically balancing robots, including BigDog, Cheetah, Atlas, and Spot, that became widely recognized demonstrations of legged robotics. Boston Dynamics passed through ownership by Google's X division, SoftBank Group, and Hyundai Motor Company over the following decades, and Raibert stepped back from the CEO role while remaining involved with the company. He now serves as Executive Director of the Robotics and AI Institute, which he leads from offices in Cambridge, Massachusetts and Zurich, Switzerland.

profiles.hook: Pieter Abbeel is a computer scientist known for his contributions to robotic learning and deep reinforcement learning. Born in Antwerp, Belgium, he studied at the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven before earning his PhD in computer science at Stanford University in 2008. He joined the faculty of UC Berkeley, where he holds the Jim Gray Chair in Engineering, directs the Berkeley Robot Learning Lab, and co-directs the Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research Lab. With his student Chelsea Finn and Sergey Levine, he co-created Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), a foundational algorithm for training models that adapt quickly to new tasks. He has also founded several companies, including the online grading platform Gradescope, the assistive robotics venture Berkeley Open Arms, and Covariant, which applies foundation models to robotic automation. His honors include the ACM Prize in Computing and IEEE Fellowship.

profiles.hook: Raquel Urtasun is a computer scientist and entrepreneur who has spent her career at the intersection of computer vision, robotics, and self driving technology. She earned her PhD in computer science from the Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne in 2006, then completed postdoctoral research at MIT and UC Berkeley before joining the Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago as an assistant professor. She later became a Canada Research Chair in Machine Learning and Computer Vision at the University of Toronto, where she remains a full professor and is a co-founder of the Vector Institute for AI. From 2017 to 2021 she served as Chief Scientist and Head of Research and Development at Uber's Advanced Technologies Group in Toronto, leading self driving vehicle research. After leaving Uber, she founded Waabi, a company building AI first software for autonomous trucks and robotaxis, where she serves as Founder and CEO.

profiles.hook: Rodney Brooks trained in pure mathematics at Flinders University in his native Australia before earning a PhD in computer science from Stanford in 1981. After research positions at Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Stanford, he joined the MIT faculty in 1984 and later directed the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and then the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. His 1986 paper describing the subsumption architecture argued that intelligent robot behavior could emerge from layered, reactive control systems rather than centralized symbolic planning, a challenge to the AI orthodoxy of the time that helped found the field of behavior-based robotics. He put that thinking into commercial practice by co-founding iRobot in 1990 with Colin Angle and Helen Greiner, whose Roomba vacuum became one of the first robots to reach mass consumer markets. In 2008 he founded Heartland Robotics, later renamed Rethink Robotics, to build the Baxter and Sawyer collaborative robots for factory work, and in 2019 he founded Robust.AI to continue work on practical, everyday robotics.

profiles.hook: Sergey Levine studied computer science at Stanford University, earning his BS and MS in 2009 and completing a PhD there in 2014. He joined the Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences faculty at UC Berkeley in 2016, where he directs the Robotic Artificial Intelligence and Learning (RAIL) lab. His research develops algorithms that let autonomous agents, especially physical robots, learn complex behaviors directly from experience using deep reinforcement learning rather than hand-engineered controllers, work that has shaped how the field approaches robotic manipulation, locomotion and autonomous vehicle control. In 2024 he joined the robotics startup Physical Intelligence, contributing to the team behind pi-zero, a general-purpose foundation model intended to control many different kinds of robots across a range of tasks.

profiles.hook: Siddhartha Srinivasa is a roboticist who describes himself as a full-stack roboticist, working across machine learning, perception, planning, and control. He spent eighteen years at Carnegie Mellon University's Robotics Institute, where in 2005 he founded the Personal Robotics Lab and developed robots including HERB and ADA, and contributed algorithms later used on NASA's Robonaut and on Mars rovers. From 2014 to 2017 he was a first-wave founder at the robotics automation startup Berkshire Grey. In 2017 he joined the University of Washington's Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering as a professor, continuing his Personal Robotics Lab research there. The following year he also took on starting and leading Amazon's Robotics AI organization, growing it to roughly four hundred people, before later serving as a Distinguished Engineer at Cruise. He is a Fellow of IEEE for his contributions to robotic manipulation and human-robot interaction, and helped write the Roadmap for US Robotics presented to Congress in 2013.

profiles.hook: Takeo Kanade earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Kyoto University in 1974 and taught there before joining Carnegie Mellon University in 1980. He directed Carnegie Mellon's Robotics Institute from 1992 to 2001 and now holds the title of U.A. and Helen Whitaker University Professor of Robotics and Computer Science there. Across a research career spanning computer vision and robotics, he pioneered early facial recognition methods, multi-baseline stereo vision, the factorization method for recovering 3D shape and motion from images, and virtualized reality techniques for capturing 3D scenes from multiple cameras. He also led Carnegie Mellon's Navlab autonomous vehicle program, including a 1995 cross-country demonstration drive in which the vehicle steered itself for most of the route from Pittsburgh to San Diego. In 2016 he received the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology for his contributions to the field.
